channel.title: FraudBad
channel.description: Fraud, waste and lost money in American government, with the receipts.

item.title: Weapons programs that went over budget this year
item.description: In one year, 46 of the Pentagon's biggest weapons programs reported $122 billion in cost increases. The average new system now takes over 12 years to deliver.

item.title: Savings the government's auditors found — and nobody took
item.description: GAO says acting on its open recommendations could save $132 billion to $251 billion. Past action on its findings has saved $774 billion since 2011.

item.title: Taxes owed that never get paid
item.description: The IRS projects $696 billion in taxes went unpaid on time for 2022. After enforcement and late payments, $606 billion is projected to go uncollected.

item.title: Social Security overpayments that haven't come back
item.description: Social Security reported $23 billion in uncollected overpayments at the start of fiscal 2024. Its inspector general later found SSA booked about $904 million as recovered that wasn't.

item.title: Food benefits skimmed straight off EBT cards
item.description: Thieves skimmed SNAP benefits off families' cards. USDA replaced $320 million from October 2022 to December 2024. Then federal replacement stopped, and so did USDA's count.

item.title: Venue grants: 69% paid wrong or without proof
item.description: SBA's Shuttered Venue Operators Grants show $14.6B in payments. In fiscal 2025, SBA counted $5.83B as improper and $4.24B it couldn't verify — 68.9% of the money, the highest rate of any program that reported.

item.title: The September rush: spend it before it expires
item.description: Agencies signed $161.9B in contracts in September 2025 — 19.5% of the year's contract money in the last month, 2.7 times an average month.

item.title: The nuclear missile that's 81% over budget
item.description: The Air Force's Sentinel ICBM is now estimated at $140.9 billion, 81% more than projected in 2020. That triggered the law for runaway weapons costs. The Pentagon kept it going.

item.title: Second Avenue subway: $7.7 billion for a mile and a half
item.description: The Second Avenue subway's extension to East Harlem — 1.5 miles and three stations — rose to $7.7 billion, about $5.1 billion a mile. The next extension west along 125th Street is also priced at $7.7 billion.

item.title: Medicare paid far more for cheap generics than an online pharmacy charges
item.description: A study in the Annals of Internal Medicine estimated Medicare could have saved $3.6 billion in a single year by paying Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company's prices for 77 generic drugs.

item.title: Paid out without proof, year after year
item.description: Federal agencies have reported $2.98 trillion in improper and unverifiable payments since fiscal 2004, by our count of the government's own dataset. Fiscal 2025 alone added $185.8B.

item.title: Rent subsidies HUD can't verify
item.description: In fiscal 2025, HUD said it couldn't determine whether $4.35B of its project-based rental assistance — 26.4% of the program — was paid correctly. A year earlier the figure was $45 million.

item.title: Honolulu's rail line: twice the cost, a mile shorter
item.description: Honolulu's elevated rail line was estimated at about $5 billion when construction began in 2011. Its official budget is now $10.079 billion, the line stops about a mile short of Ala Moana Center, and full service is targeted for 2031.

item.title: Wasted in American health care every year
item.description: About a quarter of all U.S. health spending is waste, a peer-reviewed estimate in JAMA found.

item.title: Federal tech money spent keeping old systems alive
item.description: The government spends over $100 billion a year on IT, and agencies typically put about 80% of it into running what they already have.

item.title: Money owed to the government that it isn't collecting
item.description: By the end of fiscal 2024, people and businesses owed federal agencies $217.3 billion in overdue non-tax debt. That year agencies collected $21.5 billion of overdue debt and wrote off $57.7 billion.

item.title: What the government won back from fraud in court
item.description: The Justice Department recovered more than $6.8 billion under the False Claims Act in fiscal 2025, its highest ever. Measured against GAO's fraud estimate, that's 1 to 3 cents on the dollar.

item.title: The data to stop it existed. Nobody checked.
item.description: Two-thirds of the government's $185.8B in improper payments in fiscal 2025 happened because the agency didn't check information it already had access to — by the government's own count.

item.title: Giant contracts the public can't read
item.description: 9 of the 100 biggest federal contracts active in fiscal 2026 — worth $160.4B — list no description at all, or only a filing code.

item.title: California's bullet train: $33 billion promised, up to $231 billion now
item.description: Voters approved high-speed rail in 2008 at a price of about $33 billion, done by 2020. The 2026 business plan puts San Francisco to Los Angeles at $126 billion to $231 billion. The first passengers ride in 2033, on the Central Valley segment.

item.title: Unemployment money stolen in weeks
item.description: Impostors used stolen identities to drain as much as $650 million from Washington's unemployment fund in the spring of 2020.

item.title: Refundable tax credits paid out in error
item.description: About one in four dollars of the IRS's refundable tax credits went out improperly in fiscal 2025.

item.title: Food aid paid in the wrong amount
item.description: More than one in ten SNAP dollars went out wrong in fiscal 2025.

item.title: Pandemic small-business loans that went to likely fraud
item.description: At least 17% of all Paycheck Protection Program and Covid disaster-loan money went out on potentially fraudulent applications.

item.title: Eight audits. Eight failures.
item.description: The Pentagon has tried to pass a full financial audit every year since 2018. It has never passed.

item.title: Stolen from pandemic unemployment benefits
item.description: Between 11 and 15 cents of every pandemic unemployment dollar went to fraud, GAO estimates.

item.title: Fake catheter claims using a million stolen identities
item.description: Prosecutors say one network billed Medicare $10.6 billion for medical supplies nobody needed or received.

item.title: Unemployment money New York overpaid
item.description: New York's comptroller found at least $11 billion in pandemic unemployment overpayments, including fraud.

item.title: Welfare money for the poorest, steered elsewhere
item.description: Mississippi's welfare scandal ran through TANF, the one big program left out of the federal government's improper-payment total.

item.title: Minnesota programs where prosecutors say half may be fraud
item.description: A federal prosecutor says "half or more" of the $18 billion billed to 14 high-risk Minnesota Medicaid programs since 2018 may be fraudulent. The state's own watchdog disputes it.

item.title: Fraudulent jobless claims Michigan likely paid
item.description: A consulting firm hired by the state estimated Michigan paid about $8.5 billion in fraudulent unemployment benefits in 19 months.

item.title: Health care money paid with no proof it was right
item.description: Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP paid about $95.5 billion in error in fiscal 2025. Most of it lacked the paperwork to show it was correct.

item.title: What Medicare overpays private insurance plans
item.description: Medicare's own advisers say it will pay about $76 billion more this year for people in private Medicare Advantage plans than it would in traditional Medicare.

item.title: Los Angeles hospices cut off over suspected fraud
item.description: Federal officials froze Medicare payments to hundreds of Los Angeles hospices and home health agencies in 2026.

item.title: Homelessness money LA couldn't fully trace
item.description: Court-ordered auditors identified $2.3 billion in city homelessness funding and couldn't fully quantify what was spent on each program.

item.title: Paid out in error in fiscal 2025
item.description: Federal agencies sent out $186 billion in fiscal 2025 that they shouldn't have, or couldn't prove they should have.

item.title: 455 people charged in one health care fraud sweep
item.description: In June 2026 federal prosecutors charged 455 people, including 90 doctors and other licensed professionals, over $6.5 billion in alleged false claims.

item.title: Stolen from meals for hungry kids
item.description: The largest pandemic fraud case in the country ended with its ringleader sentenced to more than 41 years.

item.title: What the government loses to fraud every year
item.description: The government's own auditors estimate fraud costs taxpayers $233 billion to $521 billion a year.

item.title: A pandemic tax credit nobody measured for fraud
item.description: The IRS paid out $283 billion through the Employee Retention Credit and never produced the fraud estimate the law requires.

item.title: Unemployment money California paid to fraudsters
item.description: California's unemployment agency told lawmakers at least $20 billion in pandemic benefits went to fraud.

item.title: Fake addiction treatment billed to Arizona Medicaid
item.description: Sham sober-living operators billed Arizona's Medicaid program for treatment that never happened, mostly targeting Native American patients.

item.title: Lost to waste, fraud and abuse rebuilding Afghanistan
item.description: The government's Afghanistan watchdog closed out its work by finding $26 billion to $29 billion of reconstruction money disappeared to waste, fraud and abuse.
